clue.text: Everything is a burden, it’s said unfailingly

indicators.note: what is said is heard, not read, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

explanation.surface: Someone sighing that life, every bit of it, is a weight to carry.
explanation.walkthrough: Say ALL WEIGHS quickly and you hear ALWAYS; the sound covers the whole phrase, not just the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfailingly means at all times, which is always.

clue.text: Glad eye? Wind-up!

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters read from the bottom

blocks.note: to reel in a line is to wind it

explanation.surface: A flirtatious look that turns out to be a tease.
explanation.walkthrough: Wind-up reads as one word meaning a joke at someone’s expense; split it and it becomes the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The glad eye is a suggestive look, and a leer is a knowing, suggestive look; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Norman Tebbit’s role – to have a go at setter?

blocks.note: to have a go at someone is to attack them
a setter is a breed of gundog

explanation.surface: A question about the politician Norman Tebbit and whether he would turn on the puzzle’s own compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter here is not Brummie but the gundog. Norman Tebbit was a combative Conservative minister, known as Margaret Thatcher’s attack dog.
explanation.definitionFit: An attack dog is a politician deployed to savage opponents, the job Tebbit did for Thatcher.

clue.text: Abandons theatre wear

blocks.note: to scrub a plan is to drop it
the loose garments worn in an operating theatre

explanation.surface: An actor walking out of the costume department.
explanation.walkthrough: Theatre suggests the stage; in Britain it is also the hospital operating theatre, where surgeons wear scrubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrubs as a verb means cancels or abandons; as a noun it is surgical clothing.

clue.text: Bat’s preparatory move, dramatically illuminated when female enters

blocks.note: lit from behind, as on a stage

explanation.surface: A night-time scene of a bat caught in stage lighting as a female flies in.
explanation.walkthrough: Bat looks like the flying animal; it is the cricket bat. The backlift is how a batsman raises the bat before a stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: The backlift is the upward movement of the bat that prepares a cricket shot.

clue.text: Cheap gibes at barman ineptly carrying measure

indicators.note: done ineptly, the letters end up in the wrong order

blocks.note: an en is a printer’s measure of width

explanation.surface: Customers mocking a bartender while he clumsily pours a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of the thirteen letters gives BARGAINBASEMT, and EN goes in near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Bargain-basement goods are the cheapest, from the discount floor of a store.

clue.text: Scam merchant gets rid of diamonds for union official

blocks.note: D = diamonds, the card suit; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: A fraudster jettisoning stolen gems to pass as a trade union man.
explanation.walkthrough: A convenor is a British trade union term for the official who calls meetings and leads shop stewards.
explanation.definitionFit: A convenor is an elected union official who organises members at a workplace.

clue.text: Bar entrance – strip clubs inside

blocks.note: a lath is a thin strip of wood

explanation.surface: A bouncer’s view of a strip club, with the bar entrance just inside.
explanation.walkthrough: Bar entrance reads as the way into a pub; it is an instruction, to bar an entrance, which is what you do when you latch a door.
explanation.definitionFit: To latch is to fasten a door, barring the entrance.

clue.text: Serious affair? No, not if trial’s rigged

explanation.surface: A courtroom remark that a case can only go one way if the trial is fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to the No: a flirtation is an affair that is not serious. The comma hides where it stops.
explanation.definitionFit: A flirtation is a light romantic dalliance, the opposite of a serious affair.

clue.text: Stop working with rock star’s ultimate fixer

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the last one

blocks.note: to rest is to stop working

explanation.surface: Someone downing tools to go and join a rock star’s crew.
explanation.walkthrough: Rock star looks like one phrase; rock is ORE and star only supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A restorer repairs old things, so is a fixer.

clue.text: Explosive agent and critic put off introducing one

indicators.note: put off its stride, the phrase is thrown into disorder
the phrase takes the one into it

explanation.surface: A saboteur and a reviewer are put off their stride by a newcomer.
explanation.walkthrough: The word and is not a link here; its three letters are part of the fodder. The answer runs on into 13 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitric acid is used to make explosives such as nitroglycerine and TNT.

clue.text: Many a flutter initiated by this US money (and a bit English)

indicators.note: the answer starts with what follows

blocks.note: cabbage is American slang for money
a whit is a tiny bit

explanation.surface: A gambler admitting that most bets are funded with dollars, plus a little sterling.
explanation.walkthrough: Flutter suggests a small bet, and US money fits that picture; but the flutter is a butterfly’s flight, and the cabbage white is a common butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabbage whites are among the commonest fluttering butterflies, so many a flutter is one.

clue.text: Divisive school is Mother Theresa’s first international college

blocks.note: sch. is the abbreviation for school

explanation.surface: A description of a controversial college, run in the name of Mother Teresa, that splits opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother Theresa looks like one name; Mother is MA and Theresa gives only its T.
explanation.definitionFit: Schismatic means causing a schism, a split, so divisive.

clue.text: See 10
Trainee mobile phone, yet complicated

explanation.surface: A new employee struggling with a work mobile that is somehow still complicated.
explanation.walkthrough: Mobile phone reads as one thing; mobile is doing the job of shuffling, alongside complicated.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: neophyte, from the Greek for newly planted, is anyone new to a skill, as a trainee is.

clue.text: Local gets in wrong rum

indicators.note: rum means odd, so the letters come out oddly arranged

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: The pub regular gets served the wrong spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: Local suggests a pub, and rum a drink; rum is the old British adjective for strange, which is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Home-grown produce or talent comes from the local area.

clue.text: United takes sending off to be lacking certification

indicators.note: letters that are off are out of order

blocks.note: U = United, as in football team names

explanation.surface: A football report: United have a player sent off.
explanation.walkthrough: Sending off is the football phrase for a red card; here the two words part company, sending as fodder and off as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A signature is what certifies a document or contract, so without one it goes uncertified.

clue.text: Pure iodine added to a tobacco

blocks.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: A chemist’s note about lacing a tobacco blend with iodine.
explanation.walkthrough: Pure looks like a description of the iodine; it is VIRGIN, and the tobacco sits at the far end as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia is a type of tobacco, named after the American state where it was grown.

clue.text: Low temperature? That’s debatable

blocks.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: Someone questioning whether a reading on the thermometer is really low.
explanation.walkthrough: Low looks like an adjective about the weather; it is the verb for the noise a cow makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A moot point is one open to debate.

clue.text: Mediocre elected president blocking measure

blocks.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits
a candidate who is elected gets in

explanation.surface: A second-rate leader, newly voted in, obstructing legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: Measure suggests a bill or policy; it is a tot, a small shot of drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinpot means inferior or second-rate, as in a tinpot dictator.

clue.text: Exaggerating what a sewer might be doing

definitions.text: what a sewer might be doing

blocks.note: to embroider a story is to add false detail

blocks.clueFragment: what a sewer might be doing
blocks.note: a sewer here is one who sews

explanation.surface: An overblown claim about what goes on in a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: A sewer reads as a drain; here it rhymes with grower and means someone who sews.
explanation.definitionFit: Embroidering means both decorating cloth with stitching and embellishing a tale.

clue.text: One who regrets welcoming Latin dictator?

explanation.surface: Someone with regrets taking in a Latin strongman.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin dictator looks like one phrase for a Roman or South American strongman; Latin supplies only its L.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictator is a ruler, and the question mark admits that not every ruler is a dictator.

clue.text: Successor’s appearance reported

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so the sound counts

blocks.note: an air is a look or manner

explanation.surface: A news item on how the heir to the throne looks.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s reads as possessive; it is the word is, joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An heir is the one who succeeds to a title or estate.

clue.text: Hot sort of scarf with neck opening

blocks.note: a stole is a long scarf worn over the shoulders

explanation.surface: A fashion note about a warm scarf with a slit for the neck.
explanation.walkthrough: Hot looks like temperature; it is slang for stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: hot goods are ones recently taken and still traceable, too risky to sell openly.

clue.text: Maybe Burton’s ex at piano, learning rock intro

explanation.surface: Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton’s ex, at the piano learning rock.
explanation.walkthrough: Burton’s ex suggests the actor Richard Burton and Elizabeth Taylor; the Burton meant is Sir Richard Burton, the Victorian explorer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Richard Francis Burton was a Victorian explorer of Africa and Arabia; maybe marks him as one example.

clue.text: One has copies, right, to correct and certify

blocks.note: cc = carbon copies; has joins it on

explanation.surface: An office clerk who holds duplicates of documents, fixing and signing them off.
explanation.walkthrough: Has is the joining word that attaches CC to the one; the commas break the chain into its pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a body that accredits a school or lab formally vouches that it meets a standard.

clue.text: Presidential term: ‘Career’s over in golf course support’

indicators.note: turned over, the word reads backwards

blocks.note: a tee holds the ball up on a golf course
a career is a run of work

explanation.surface: A headline declaring a president’s career finished while he is off playing golf.
explanation.walkthrough: Career’s over reads as a verdict on a politician; read the ’s as is, and over becomes the instruction to turn the career round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenure is the period during which an office, such as a presidency, is held.
